sections.title: Head and face idioms
sections.content:
Many English idioms use parts of the body figuratively:
• keep a straight face — avoid laughing. I couldn't keep a straight face when he told the joke.
• off the top of my head — without thinking carefully. Off the top of my head, I'd say there are about fifty.
• turn a blind eye — pretend not to notice. The manager turned a blind eye to the employees arriving late.
• see eye to eye — agree completely. We don't always see eye to eye on politics.
• bite your tongue — stop yourself from saying something. I had to bite my tongue to avoid arguing with her.

sections.title: Hand and arm idioms
sections.content:
Idioms involving hands and arms:
• lend a hand — help someone. Could you lend me a hand with these boxes?
• get out of hand — become uncontrollable. The party got completely out of hand.
• keep at arm's length — maintain distance from someone. She keeps her work colleagues at arm's length.
• twist someone's arm — persuade someone reluctantly. I didn't want to go, but she twisted my arm.
• wash your hands of — refuse further responsibility. After years of trying, he washed his hands of the project.

sections.title: Other body idioms
sections.content:
More idioms using body parts:
• cold feet — nervousness before an important event. She got cold feet before the wedding.
• break a leg — good luck (especially in performance). You're on stage tonight? Break a leg!
• get something off your chest — say something that's been worrying you. I need to get something off my chest — I disagree with the plan.
• have a gut feeling — have an intuitive sense. I have a gut feeling this deal isn't right.

exercises.question: 'She turned a blind eye to the problem' means she:
exercises.explanation: Turn a blind eye means to deliberately ignore something you know is wrong.

exercises.question: If a situation 'gets out of hand', it becomes:
exercises.explanation: Get out of hand means to become difficult to manage or control.

exercises.question: Having 'cold feet' before an event means feeling:
exercises.explanation: Cold feet means a loss of nerve or confidence before an important event.

exercises.question: 'Off the top of my head' means answering:
exercises.hint: You haven't thought about it deeply.
exercises.explanation: Off the top of my head means saying something without much thought or research.

exercises.question: To 'bite your tongue' means to:
exercises.explanation: Bite your tongue means to make a deliberate effort not to say something.

exercises.question: To 'twist someone's arm' means to:
exercises.explanation: Twist someone's arm means to persuade someone to do something they're reluctant to do.

exercises.question: A 'gut feeling' is a feeling based on:
exercises.explanation: A gut feeling is an instinctive feeling, as opposed to an opinion based on facts.

exercises.question: To 'get something off your chest' means to:
exercises.hint: Finally saying what's been bothering you.
exercises.explanation: Get something off your chest means to say something that has been worrying you.
